The greedy maximal matching takes edge 2–3 first (accent); every other edge touches 2 or 3, so nothing more can be added, even though the larger matching 1–2, 3–4 exists. The card shows the returned edge id 1, the pair 2–3, and size 1." width="100%"} A maximal matching is a matching (set of edges with no shared endpoints) that cannot be extended by adding any other edge. Uses a greedy algorithm that scans edges in creation (edge ID) order, so the result is deterministic for a given graph but can change if the same edges are added in a different order. Note that a maximal matching is not necessarily a maximum matching (largest possible). For weighted graphs, use `maximum_weight_matching()`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of edge IDs forming a maximal matching. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Runs a greedy scan of the edge list in $O(E)$: each edge whose endpoints are both still unmatched joins the matching and marks them off. The result is *maximal* in the inclusion-ordering sense (no further edge can be added without a conflict) but not necessarily *maximum*: a matching that ties up the wrong endpoints first can leave more edges dangling than an optimal one would. For maximum cardinality matching on general graphs, Edmonds' blossom algorithm runs in $O(V \cdot E)$ but is far more elaborate; for bipartite inputs, Hopcroft-Karp's $O(E \sqrt{V})$ is the workhorse. When edge weights matter, `maximum_weight_matching()` handles the objective-aware variant. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A path of 6 nodes has exactly 3 disjoint edges available, so a maximal matching pairs every node: ::: {#35bc1bc4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_path_graph(6) # 1-2-3-4-5-6 matching = graph.maximal_matching() # Returns 3 (e.g., edges 1-2, 3-4, 5-6) len(matching) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: The matched edges can be marked as an edge attribute for a quick visual check of which connections were paired up: ::: {#9e43a0d9 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_grid_2d(rows=4, cols=4) matching = graph.maximal_matching() # Color matched edges for visualization colors = {edge_id: "red" for edge_id in matching} graph.set_edge_attrs("color", colors) # Returns the number of matched edges len(matching) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 8 ``` ::: ::: In a complete graph with an even number of nodes, a maximal matching is also a perfect matching, pairing every single node: ::: {#64c242cc .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_full_graph(10) matching = graph.maximal_matching() # Returns 5 (all 10 nodes paired up) len(matching) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 5 ``` ::: :::
